title: RMF Checklist Automation
tagline: Python tools that made a defense contractor's quarterly security reports faster and safer
summary: My first internship was at TTM Technologies, a defense contractor, in the summer of 2024. Their cybersecurity team had to update big checklist files by hand every quarter for compliance reports. I built three small Python apps that do most of that work, with a review step in the middle so nothing changes without a person seeing it first.

hero.alt: NIST Risk Management Framework and DISA STIG marks representing the two standards connected by the project
hero.caption: The two standards the project connects: NIST RMF and DISA STIGs.

sections.heading: The problem
body: Defense systems have to follow a set of security rules called the NIST Risk Management Framework, and DISA publishes checklists, called STIGs, that turn those rules into specific checks. A scan fills in part of the checklist, but the rest needs a person to mark each finding with a reason, and those decisions were spread across spreadsheets. Doing it by hand every quarter was slow and easy to mess up.

sections.heading: Learning it first
body: I didn't know any of this going in, so I started by running a scan on my own computer and following how everything moved through the checklist file. After talking with the team, I sketched the whole thing out on a whiteboard. The big decision was to split it into three steps, with a person reviewing in the middle.

media.alt: Flowchart showing a STIG export, required controls, optional exclusions and the current CKL feeding a review CSV, followed by Answer File XML and a validated CKL with a run log
media.caption: The three steps, with a review in the middle.

sections.heading: Three small apps
body: The first app compares the scan results with the controls the system actually needs, and makes a spreadsheet of findings that probably don't apply, with the reason for each one. Someone reviews and edits that spreadsheet. The second app turns the approved spreadsheet into an answer file, and the third applies those answers to the checklist.

media.alt: AnswerFile Excel Gen desktop window with inputs for RMF control lists, a STIG export and an original CKL, plus configurable status and comment rules
media.caption: Step 1: build the review spreadsheet.

media.alt: Excel to AF desktop window with fields for the reviewed answers CSV, STIG name and answer key
media.caption: Step 2: turn the approved answers into an answer file.

media.alt: CKL Modifier desktop window with Answer File and CKL inputs, comment placeholders, log filters and a detailed modification report
media.caption: Step 3: update the checklist and log every change.

sections.heading: Never overwrite something newer
body: The part I'm happiest with is a safety check. Each answer remembers what the finding's status was when it was reviewed. If the checklist says something different by the time the answer is applied, the app leaves it alone and reports it instead of overwriting newer data. It also logs every change, every skip, and anything that looked wrong.

sections.heading: How it went
body: I wrote everything with Python's standard library and Tkinter, since fewer outside packages is easier in a security-focused place. It started as command-line experiments and turned into these apps after feedback from the team. They used it for five quarterly reports. If I did it again, I'd clean up the code so the three apps share one XML helper instead of each having its own copy.
